transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—thanks for coming. Can you tell me what's been bringing you in today?

Well… honestly, what finally pushed me to make the appointment is that it’s starting to interfere with things I really need to be able to track at work. I manage health services, so I’m in EPIC reports and clinic metrics meetings all the time, and I’ll sit down with every intention of paying attention—like, I’m ready, I’ve got the report open, I know it matters—and then within a few minutes my mind is just… gone somewhere else.

And then I realize I’m rereading the same line of numbers over and over, or I’ve been looking at the screen but not actually absorbing any of it. In meetings it’s worse sometimes because I’ll suddenly realize people have been discussing something important and I’ve missed the whole point of what was said. It’s embarrassing, and it’s frustrating, because I’m not trying to check out. I really do care about the work. It just feels like my attention slips away before I even notice it’s happening.
Thinking back, did you notice similar problems with attention and staying focused when you were a kid or teenager, or is this something that's really only shown up recently?

No, it’s definitely not brand new. I mean, it feels more obvious now because my work is so detail-heavy, but when I think back, there were signs pretty early.

Even in elementary school, I remember teachers writing things like I was “bright but careless,” which I heard a lot. It wasn’t that I couldn’t understand the work—I usually could—but I’d miss instructions or forget part of what I was supposed to do. My mother used to have to sit with me while I finished homework, not because she needed to teach it to me exactly, but because I’d drift off or lose track of what assignment I was even doing. And I’d forget books at school, or bring home the wrong thing, and then we’d have this whole evening of trying to figure out how I was supposed to finish something without the right materials.

So yes, when I look back, it was there. I think I just got labeled as careless or not applying myself, rather than anyone seeing it as a consistent attention problem.

Growing up, and even now, would you describe yourself as someone who was fidgety, restless, or often acted impulsively—like interrupting others or making quick decisions without thinking them through?

I’m not really sure I’d describe myself that way, no. I mean, I can get mentally restless, I guess, but if you mean like physically fidgety or constantly needing to move around, that’s not something people have usually said about me.

As a kid, I don’t remember being the one who was bouncing out of my seat or getting in trouble for disrupting the class. And even now, I don’t think of myself as especially impulsive. I’m usually pretty cautious, sometimes probably too much so. I don’t tend to just blurt things out or make big snap decisions without thinking—at least not in any way that stands out to me.

I may have to think about it more, but my main issue has always felt more like… losing the thread, not being unable to sit still.
Outside of work, do you notice this same kind of losing track of things or zoning out—like at home, during conversations, or while doing personal tasks such as paying bills or reading?

Yes, I do, although the place it feels most obvious—and honestly the most upsetting—is still work. That’s the part that finally pushed me to come in, because it’s not just an annoyance anymore.

Like, I’ll open an EPIC quality report, and I really do mean to focus. I’m not avoiding it, I’m not thinking, “Oh, I don’t care about this.” I’ll have the report pulled up, maybe a notebook next to me, and I’ll be trying to follow the clinic metrics or compare numbers, and then within a few minutes it’s like my mind has slipped sideways. I’ll suddenly realize I’ve been staring at the same row of numbers and rereading it over and over, but I haven’t actually taken it in.

And in meetings it’s similar. I can be sitting there in a clinic metrics meeting trying to track what everyone’s saying, and then all of a sudden I realize I missed the whole point of the discussion. Like people have moved on, or someone is asking about next steps, and I’m trying to piece together what was just decided from context clues. It’s really uncomfortable, because I’m there, I’m looking attentive, but internally I’ve lost the thread.

So yes, it’s that same kind of zoning out or losing track—mostly I notice it when I need to sustain attention on something detailed for more than a few minutes. It makes me feel embarrassed, because these are things I should be able to follow.

Can you give me a specific example of how this attention trouble affects you at home—like when you're paying bills, reading something for yourself, or trying to keep track of personal appointments and tasks?

At home, the closest example is probably when I sit down to do something that should be straightforward but has a lot of little details—like going through a statement or trying to track something in a portal. I’ll have it open and I really am intending to deal with it, but then I realize I’ve been looking at the same section over and over and I’m not actually absorbing it.

It’s very similar to what happens at work, honestly. What finally made me come in is that I can start an EPIC quality report or sit in a clinic metrics meeting with every intention of following along, and within a few minutes my mind has drifted so far that I’m rereading the same numbers or realizing I missed the whole point of what people were discussing. At home it feels like the same mechanism, just maybe with less immediate consequence—like I can put the paper down and come back later—but it still makes simple tasks take much longer than they should.

And it’s not that I don’t care or I’m choosing not to focus. That’s the frustrating part. I’ll be sitting there thinking, “Okay, just read this carefully,” and then a few minutes later I’m sort of waking up to the fact that I haven’t actually been with it.

Would you say these attention difficulties have actually caused real problems—like mistakes at work, missed deadlines, or conflict at home—or is it more that they're frustrating but haven't led to concrete negative consequences?

It has started causing real problems, yes. I think for a while I was telling myself it was just frustrating or inefficient, like, “Okay, I’m slower with these reports than I should be,” but lately it’s been harder to explain it away that way.

At work, the delays have actually started affecting clinic reporting deadlines. I’ll need to get a quality report or some clinic metrics information pulled together, and because I keep losing the thread and having to reread or recheck things, it takes me much longer than it should. Then other teams are waiting on me, which feels awful because I know their work depends on having that information. It’s not just me sitting there annoyed with myself anymore—it creates a bottleneck.

And outside of my main job, I’ve also had to step back from leading parts of the volunteer health workshops I help with. I used to be more involved in keeping the planning pieces moving, but I haven’t felt reliable with it. There are too many details to track, and if I don’t stay on top of them, other people are left scrambling or checking behind me. So I’ve pulled back from leading those parts, which is embarrassing, because I do care about it and I want to contribute. I just can’t consistently keep all the moving pieces moving the way I need to.
